nodes.title: Kill-tested 6 times mid-write: state always parseable, ledger never torn, but 3 of 6 kills leaked a stray .tmp
nodes.body:
Tested the durability claim directly instead of reasoning about it: spawned a writer that loop-publishes state with writeJsonAtomic and appends to a JSONL ledger, then SIGKILLed it at six random points (120-320 ms in, after 30-70 writes each).

Results: the state file was always parseable (6/6), and the ledger had zero torn lines across ~300 appended records. So the temp-then-rename publish is doing its job for the reader: a crashed write never exposes a half-written state. That part of our design holds.

Two holes the same test found:
(1) rename-over-open-reader fails on Windows with EPERM (measured separately in e16.mjs), so a panel HTTP request holding the state file open can make the loop's own publish throw. Our reader does not hold it, so there is no live incident -- but the failure mode is a lost round, not a retry.
(2) 3 of 6 kills left a stray .tmp file behind, because nothing cleans them up. They accumulate under ~/.dsh/loom until a human notices. Cheap fix: sweep *.tmp at boot in recovery, alongside the lesson retirement that already happens there.
(3) The helper does not fsync. rename is atomic against a process crash but not against a power loss: the rename can be visible while the file contents are still in the page cache. For a local single-user tool that is an acceptable trade (a lost round is recoverable from the ledger, which is the actual authority), but it should be a stated trade rather than an oversight.

The deeper point: state.json is derived. The ledger is authoritative and rebuild() reproduces state. So the correct durability fix is not a stronger state write, it is making sure boot always rebuilds from the ledger rather than trusting a state file that might be stale or missing -- and that is already what recovery does.

edges.note: Confirms rename is unsafe only with a concurrent open reader (EPERM) and never exposes a torn target.
The ledger being authoritative is what makes a weak state publish acceptable.
Durability belongs in boot-time rebuild, not in a stronger atomic write.
